The final Dutch GP at Zandvoort is underway.

Ferrari led FP1. Sprint Qualifying up next (16:30 CEST).

One practice. One chance. This Sprint weekend is going to be wild. 🇳🇱

#DutchGP #F1 #Zandvoort

facebook.long_form:
Window: 10:00 AM ET

Ferrari came to the final Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort and immediately made a statement — topping Friday's FP1 session to go 1-2 on the timing sheets.

That matters more than it normally would, because this Sprint weekend means teams had just one 60-minute practice session before Sprint Qualifying at 16:30 CEST. No second practice. No second chance to fine-tune the setup. Whatever data Ferrari gathered in that session is essentially all they have before the grid locks in for the Sprint Race.

Mercedes was also in the mix — as they have been for much of the 2026 season — keeping the championship fight tight on a circuit that has historically suited different aerodynamic profiles. The 2026 cars are making their first appearance at Zandvoort; there's no historical baseline for teams to reference.

Sprint Qualifying results are coming in this afternoon. We'll have a full update on grid positions shortly.

This is the final Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort. The circuit won't appear on the F1 calendar again. The orange army is out in force, and whatever happens over the next two days will be the last memories made at this circuit in Formula 1. Ferrari leading FP1 is exactly the kind of detail that makes the buildup feel electric.

Are you watching the Dutch GP this weekend? 🇳🇱

BREAKING: Isack Hadjar is OUT of the Dutch GP with a wrist injury (boxing gym, summer break).

Liam Lawson steps up to race Red Bull.
Yuki Tsunoda — who Hadjar replaced — returns to Racing Bulls.

The drama never stops. 🤯

#F1 #DutchGP

x_posts.label: Post 2-2
x_posts.text:
Yuki Tsunoda is BACK in an F1 car this weekend.

Hadjar's wrist injury forces a reshuffle: Lawson gets the Red Bull seat. Tsunoda returns to Racing Bulls — the same team he was bumped from to make way for Hadjar.

What a storyline. 🏎️

#F1 #DutchGP

facebook.long_form:
Window: 8:00 AM ET

Formula 1 just gave us one of its most dramatic pre-race storylines of the season — and it happened without a wheel turning in anger.

Isack Hadjar is out of the Dutch Grand Prix. The young Red Bull driver suffered a wrist injury during the summer break, sustained during a boxing session at the gym. He's been cleared unfit to race this weekend.

What follows from that single injury is a remarkable chain of events:

Liam Lawson, who has been waiting in the wings, steps up to race the senior Red Bull car at Zandvoort.

And Yuki Tsunoda — who was displaced from Red Bull Racing at the start of 2026 specifically to make room for Hadjar — returns to the Racing Bulls seat alongside Arvid Lindblad.

Think about the symmetry there. Tsunoda lost his Red Bull seat to Hadjar. Hadjar gets hurt. Tsunoda comes back at the same race, racing for the junior team, while the driver who replaced him races the senior car.

F1 doesn't script these things. They just happen.

For Lawson, this is the opportunity he's been hoping for. A race in the Red Bull at a Sprint weekend, at one of the sport's most atmospheric circuits, with the whole paddock watching.

How do you think Lawson and Tsunoda will perform this weekend? 👇

---

article.headline: Hadjar Out With Wrist Injury: Lawson Races Red Bull, Tsunoda Makes Surprise Return at Dutch GP

stories.title: Verstappen's 2030 Extension — Quotes, Context, What It Really Means (Tier 2)

x_posts.label: Post 3
x_posts.text:
Verstappen, on his Red Bull extension through 2030:

"We have the best people and I'm excited to keep working together to get back to the top again."

Exit clauses: gone. McLaren talks: dead.

The Verstappen saga is officially over. ✅

#F1 #RedBull

facebook.long_form:
Window: 12:00 PM ET

The most analyzed, debated, and speculated-about contract situation in recent Formula 1 history has finally come to an end.

Max Verstappen is staying at Red Bull. Through 2030.

He announced the extension on Thursday, perfectly timed ahead of his home Dutch Grand Prix. The previous deal — signed before the 2026 season — ran through 2028 and contained performance-based exit clauses that had fueled 18 months of intense speculation about where Verstappen might go. McLaren, Mercedes, and others were linked at various points. McLaren's Zak Brown had already confirmed talks "didn't go anywhere."

Now those clauses are dead. Verstappen isn't going anywhere.

His quote on the extension: "I am really pleased with the contract extension. We have the best people and I'm excited to keep working together with everyone to get back to the top again."

Team principal Laurent Mekies responded: "Having Max continue with us and retaining the best driver on the grid is fantastic news for everyone at Red Bull, Oracle Red Bull Racing, as well as F1 and motorsport as a whole."

There's something revealing about the phrase "get back to the top again." Red Bull dominated 2023 and early 2024; the 2026 regulation change disrupted them, and Verstappen himself hinted earlier this year about the possibility of stepping away from F1 over dissatisfaction with the new-spec cars. The fact that he's committing to 2030 suggests he believes Red Bull has a genuine path back to the front.

This weekend at Zandvoort — his home race, the first race since the announcement — will be fascinating to watch.

---

article.headline: Verstappen's 2030 Extension: What the Quotes Reveal — and What the End of the Saga Really Means

stories.title: Carlos Sainz Williams Multi-Year — Why He Chose to Stay (Tier 2)

x_posts.label: Post 4
x_posts.text:
Carlos Sainz had options — Audi, Aston Martin were both on the table.

He chose to stay at Williams.

Multi-year extension signed. Sainz betting on James Vowles' project.

Sainz + Albon. Williams' 2027 lineup is set. 💪

#F1 #Williams

facebook.long_form:
Window: 5:00 PM ET

Carlos Sainz had choices. Real ones.

Audi. Aston Martin. Both were reportedly on the table when his Williams contract situation came to a head this summer. And after his two-podium debut season in 2025 — when he helped Williams finish 5th in the Constructors' Championship — Sainz had proved he could drive for anyone.

He chose to stay.

Williams confirmed a multi-year extension (the exact length wasn't disclosed) this week, completing their 2027 driver lineup. Alex Albon had extended just one day earlier, keeping the Albon-Sainz partnership together.

The decision is a significant vote of confidence in team principal James Vowles, who has been rebuilding Williams methodically since arriving from Mercedes. The 2026 season under the new regulations has been tougher — Williams sits 9th in the Constructors' standings — but the trajectory since Vowles' arrival has been clearly upward.

Sainz, 32, is betting that trajectory continues. He knows Vowles. He's seen the investment Williams is making. And having won Grands Prix with Ferrari and driven alongside champions throughout his career, he presumably has a clear sense of where this team is headed.

The silly season's biggest open questions are now resolved: Ferrari (Hamilton/Leclerc), McLaren (Norris/Piastri), Mercedes (Russell/Antonelli), Red Bull (Verstappen/pending), Williams (Sainz/Albon) for 2027. The grid is taking shape.

Would you have made the same call as Sainz? 👇

---

article.headline: Carlos Sainz Signs Multi-Year Williams Extension — Why He Chose Grove Over Audi and Aston Martin

Kimi Antonelli is 50 points clear in the F1 championship.

He's 21 years old.

If he holds on and wins this title, he becomes the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history. 👀

Round 12 starts NOW at Zandvoort.

#F1 #DutchGP

facebook.long_form:
Window: 2:00 PM ET

When the Dutch Grand Prix takes the green flag Sunday at Zandvoort, here's the championship picture:

Kimi Antonelli, 21 years old, leads with 219 points. He has 6 wins, 6 poles, and 9 podiums in 11 races. He drives for Mercedes. He is chasing his first World Championship.

Lewis Hamilton, in his first season with Ferrari, sits 50 points back at 169. George Russell, Antonelli's own teammate, is 59 behind at 160.

What makes Antonelli's position remarkable is not just the points gap — it's the consistency. Six poles, nine podiums: the numbers say he hasn't just won races, he's converted his advantages almost every time he's had them. That's not luck. That's a driver in total command of his machinery and his racecraft.

316 points are still available over the remaining 12 rounds. Hamilton and Russell are both mathematically very much in it. Ferrari's two-phase upgrade plan — new aero at Zandvoort, ADUO-2 engine at Monza — is specifically designed to chip away at this gap.

But Antonelli comes into Round 12 leading. At Zandvoort, on a Sprint weekend, where the margin for error is smallest.

Who's your pick to win the 2026 F1 World Championship? ⬇️

---

article.headline: Antonelli's 50-Point Lead: The Championship Picture Heading Into the Dutch Grand Prix
